title: Bendigo to spend $70m on clean-up
full_text:
Bendigo Bank faces a $70m clean-up bill and years of remedial work after the prudential regulator imposed new licence conditions on the lender – stopping short of heavy sanctions – over its persistent failure to address non-financial risk.
The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority has imposed new licence conditions on Bendigo Bank after finding “longstanding and pervasive weaknesses” in the bank’s handling of non-financial risk and finding that it failed to do enough about it. APRA said it would require Bendigo Bank to maintain its $50m capital penalty, imposed last year, until it was satisfied the bank could improve.
The latest action against Bendigo Bank comes after APRA hit the bank with an $8m fine last week, finding it had weak technology controls and cyber-security systems, after a hacker breached the bank’s accounts and stole hundreds of thousands of dollars from customers.
Last year, APRA imposed the $50m capital penalty after Bendigo Bank faced an investigation by Austrac over concerns its community branches had allegedly become embroiled in organised crime.
APRA said it had reviewed a root cause analysis of Bendigo Bank’s failings, after the bank revealed last year issues around its handling of money-laundering issues. The Deloitte review, APRA said, had found Bendigo Bank had prevalent issues of weak management of non-financial risk.
Further, APRA found Bendigo Bank did not have “a clear, complete and reliable view of its regulatory obligations, material risks and key controls”.
The bank was also found to have “material deficiencies in governance, accountability, compliance management, risk oversight and risk management capability”.
APRA said it was “not satisfied that the bank has addressed the underlying root causes of its risk management deficiencies or delivered sustainable risk uplift”.
The new licence conditions imposed on Bendigo Bank require it to undertake a new rectification program and bring in independent assurance to fix its risk failures.
APRA deputy chair Therese McCarthy Hockey said the regulator was seriously concerned about weaknesses at Bendigo Bank. “Although Bendigo Bank is financially sound, with strong capital and liquidity positions, APRA is concerned with the gaps in its non-financial risk management framework,” she said. “The weaknesses identified by the root cause analysis are significant, longstanding and require decisive action.” Bendigo Bank told investors its risk remediation plan, after orders from the prudential regulator, would cost at least $70m and take more than three years.
Bendigo Bank chief executive Richard Fenell said a review of the lender had shown “our current non-financial risk management capabilities are clearly not where they need to be”.
“Our risk rectification plan will be designed to drive a fundamental shift in our management of non-financial risk,” he said. Mr Fenell on Tuesday told analysts Bendigo Bank would attempt to rein in its expenses growth despite the added cost of the remediation plan.
